extracted.intended_audience: research funders, grant administrators, policy-makers, and researchers studying peer review and funding processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing peer review and funding decision processes for research grants (reviewer selection, scoring, panel composition, applicant burden, and funder workflows). Targets funders, administrators and researchers seeking evidence-based interventions to improve reliability, fairness, and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-selection algorithm that incorporates funder guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a network flow theory algorithm to assign proposals to reviewers by incorporating the funder’s own guidelines (for instance, the number of reviewers per proposal, how many external or internal, and the restrictions on memberships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piloting matched 83 proposals with reviewers without conflict of interest (Council of Natural Sciences); outcome on review quality unknown. Useful for operationalising explicit funder constraints into assignment; monitor downstream review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow researcher nominations of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to scrap researcher nominations of reviewers to reduce bias in selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ARC recommended this as part of measures to improve reliability; to be combined with other measures such as assigning more reviewers and improving interrater agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning more than two reviewers per proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the number of reviewers per application improves interrater agreement; NIH simulation identified an 'ideal' of four reviewers, with at least three suggested as a compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps reliably score contentious/risky applications and supports funding innovative research (CMOC 3). Agency-wide implementation may be difficult; smaller funders may struggle to find reviewers. Balance reliability gains against resource and administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign more proposals to each reviewer to improve interrater agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving interrater agreement by assigning more proposals per reviewer (i.e., increasing sample per rater).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ARC recommended this to improve interrater agreement. Benefit must be weighed against exacerbating reviewer fatigue (see CMOC 9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many reviewers per application to reduce chance and outlier effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a high number of independent reviewers (e.g., 11) and an independent ranking method can prevent outlier reviews from skewing final scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McGill study showed greater reliability but managerial, administrative time and cost implications may be large; evidence of implementation at scale was not found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involving applicants in the peer review process (applicant-reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate applicants to rank competing proposals (e.g., applicants each ranked seven proposals), with scoring safeguards to prevent sabotage and bonus incentives for honest alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF pilot reported reviews similar in quality to external experts and created a motivated reviewer pool; concerns remain that emphasizing group consensus may discourage innovative ideas (CMOC 3). Quality beyond interrater agreement often unmeasured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training reviewers to improve interrater reliability and review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide reviewer training (various modalities) to increase scoring accuracy, interrater reliability, and time spent understanding review criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ RCT found modality matters: self-taught electronic package improved review quality more than a taught workshop; effects may not be long-term. An 11-minute video increased reliability for novice and experienced reviewers (Sattler et al.). Recommend repeated/follow-up training and focus areas like defining review criteria and appropriate use of rating scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ two independent review panels for the same applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two independent panels to score applications to improve interrater agreement and reliability of funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NHMRC RCT found improved agreement and reduced emphasis on track record, which can discourage bias against early career researchers and innovation (positive unintended effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify scoring systems (dichotomous vs scale-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace multi-point scale-based scores with dichotomous scores (e.g., yes/no) to simplify review while maintaining reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University of Texas/GPRF evaluation suggested dichotomous scoring is equally reliable but simpler. Simpler scoring may shorten discussions and reduce reviewer cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average opposing expert opinions and collate reviews in one report
rubrics_metrics.description: When two experts hold highly opposing opinions, averaging their scores and collating reviews into one combined report can bridge epistemological differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational study (Academy of Finland) supports this approach and highlights the importance of diversifying panels to obtain multidisciplinary expertise (CMOC 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify review panels for multidisciplinary expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble panels with a range of expertise to combine individual areas and bridge epistemological differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports reliable review processes; cited as complement to collating reviews and reducing bias; recommended where proposals span disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote community engagement via applicant and reviewer training
rubrics_metrics.description: Educate early career researchers on community engagement and provide clearer guidance on community engagement review and funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH piloted workgroups including public members and patient representatives to redefine 'community engagement' and develop guidance criteria, later producing a community engagement framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include public members, patients and stakeholders in decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Use External Community Review Committees or two-tier review systems where scientific review is followed by stakeholder/consumer review (or stakeholders have equal authority) to increase community relevance and translational impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECRC at ICTR selected nine projects that expert review had not; PCORI and MICHR showed improved translational/social relevance. Risks: consumers may lack technical expertise—mitigate by gating consumer review to scientifically vetted proposals or providing intensive training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community engagement scoring criteria: involvement, priority, benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Score community engagement using dimensions such as 'involvement, priority, and benefit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MICHR model used these criteria and is transferable to other funders wishing to incorporate community relevance into scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorten applications and limit technical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use shorter application formats (e.g., 1,200-word summaries, 2–4 page synopses, or reduced page Research Plans) focusing on research question, methodology, budget, partnerships and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AusHSI found increases in shortlisting and interview invitations; NIH shortened R01 research plan from 25 to 12 pages to focus on big picture; Villum Foundation used three-page summaries and anonymisation to 'fund ideas not pedigree'. Reviewers can request more info if needed; shorter formats reduce applicant burden and may reduce emphasis on track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide timely and meaningful feedback to applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver additional, constructive feedback (automated summaries, reviewer comments, committee summaries) early—ideally after triage or before funding committee decisions—so applicants can improve resubmissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ProGrid produced automated summary feedback well-received by applicants. Three rounds of online peer feedback correlated with improved application quality between first and second rounds (National Taiwan University study). Timing of feedback matters (earlier is better).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access to peer review comments among reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Make reviewers’ comments accessible to other reviewers to encourage accountability, constructive critique, and modification of unfair comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital Humanities Conference reforms encouraged thoughtful critique and cross-community review; applicability in health funding uncertain and may face cultural resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support applicants' grant-writing skills via outreach and mentoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders provide workshops, outreach presentations, mentoring programmes, networking and publicise institutional submission/success rates to improve proposal alignment with funder priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BP’s Venture Research Unit and NSF outreach demonstrated improved proposal quality and higher return on investment; funder-led support reduces unnecessary applicant burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate applicants about funding processes via internal training programmes
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions run internal funding programmes and courses to train students and staff in proposal writing and peer review to increase success rates and understanding of funding systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georgetown, University of Wisconsin, and National Taiwan University examples showed improved success rates, external investment, publications and participant learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote applications from new investigators (NI/Early Stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce 'New Investigator' flags, special awards and tailored review considerations to focus on research novelty and training environment rather than prior grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NI tick box on NIH R01 enabled focus on novelty and environment; pilot success rates similar to established investigators. Complemented with Early Stage Investigator and Pathway to Independence awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimise review structures (redistribute sections, match expertise, monitor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reorganise study sections/review groups to better align reviewer expertise to applications and monitor matching quality over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH restructuring redistributed basic science sections to larger study sections, alleviating pressure and improving matching; periodic re-evaluation recommended when implementing other interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use virtual panels and implement reviewer rotation policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace some in-person meetings with virtual panels, shorten reviewer terms, allow breaks, and require mandatory step-down periods after consecutive service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH and NSF piloted virtual panels to reduce costs; Marie Sklodowska-Curie Actions found no effect on interrater reliability. AMRC recommends 6 years on, 3 years off; ad hoc reviewers can bring fresh insight. Virtual panels reduce cost and can help reduce reviewer fatigue if panel size adjusted appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application triage to manage review load
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement realistic triage mechanisms to reject low-chance applications early, matching demand to funding availability and clarifying expectations for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RAND/CIHR recommendations emphasised triage and the need to clarify expectations on feedback post-triage to support reviewers and applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control application demand via submission limits and quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit submissions per applicant or institution, use invitation-only full proposals, or cooling-off periods to reduce administrative burden and encourage institutional triage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH limited applicants to one R01 per cycle historically; NSF used quotas on preliminary/full proposals and invitations. Such policies reduce funder burden but may shift burden to institutions and increase internal competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce internal peer review at applicants' institutions before external submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Require or encourage faculty/internal peer scoring of proposals prior to external submission to improve quality and interdisciplinary output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University of Pittsburgh Department of Psychiatry implemented internal review; impact on external success not published but interdisciplinary publications increased. Could increase internal competition among applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt automation and compliance checking to streamline processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use automated proposal compliance checking systems and virtual infrastructure to simplify application processing and redirect administrative capacity to merit review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF planned automated compliance checking and virtual panel standardisation; reported cost savings from virtual panels and potential efficiency gains from automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhance the reviewer pool (expand reviewers, allocate more reviewers per proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase number and diversity of reviewers, allocate more reviewers per proposal and use group consensus methods to reduce burden and increase fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulations (University of Wisconsin) suggest benefits only when funding demand is also reduced; feasibility depends on reducing submissions or increasing reviewer recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decision models and software to support funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ decision-support tools (e.g., ProGrid, Teamworker) that use performance matrices and algorithms to integrate reviewer scores, detect inconsistencies, and generate summary reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ProGrid used criteria such as academic record, research experience, reference letters, supervisor background, trainee's role, overall merit, and training environment. Software can make decisions more objective, consistent and shorten committee discussions; repurposing possible for promotions and other evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis of applicant CVs to predict research success
rubrics_metrics.description: Model relationships between CV metrics and review outcomes to predict likelihood of success and inform shortlisting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spanish SRA used statistical analysis to identify 'good' applicants based on productivity metrics; recommended optimising decision tools to support shortlisting while being mindful of potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamline funding cycles and simplify review outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Accelerate funding cycles (short windows), shorten applications, and use simplified triage outcomes (e.g., 'reject', 'revise', 'accept to interview') to reduce funder and applicant burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AusHSI accelerated two-month process increased efficiency and reduced administrative cost; reported reduced emphasis on track record as a positive unintended effect. Extend resubmission deadlines to allow applicants time to respond to earlier feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify composition of review and decision panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the makeup of panels (size, stakeholder representation, balance of internal/external reviewers) to achieve desired review culture and priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as a commonly implemented incremental change by funders; can be used to promote innovation, co-funding, ECR support, and diversification of perspectives across funding decisions.
